questions.question: Define chemical equilibrium, explain why it is described as dynamic, and explain why it can only be established in a closed system. Include how the equilibrium first arises from the moment reactants are mixed.
questions.expected_answer: Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction, in a closed system, in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so that the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. It is dynamic because both the forward and reverse reactions continue at the particle level — molecules react in both directions every instant — while the macroscopic totals stay unchanged; the reaction has not stopped. It requires a closed system (one that exchanges energy but not matter with the surroundings) because if products escaped, the reverse reaction would lose its ingredients and its rate could never rise to match the forward rate. The equilibrium arises as follows: initially reactant concentrations are high, so the forward rate is high, while no products exist and the reverse rate is zero; as products accumulate the reverse rate increases while the forward rate falls as reactants are consumed, until the two rates become equal — from that moment the concentrations remain constant. Note that constant concentrations do not mean equal concentrations: the equilibrium mixture can lie far to either side.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. For the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with the forward reaction exothermic, predict and explain the effect on the ammonia yield of (a) increasing the pressure, (b) increasing the temperature, (c) removing ammonia continuously, and (d) adding an iron catalyst. Explain why industry uses a moderate temperature.
questions.expected_answer: Le Chatelier's principle: when the equilibrium in a closed system is disturbed, the system re-instates a new equilibrium by favouring the reaction that opposes the disturbance. (a) Increasing pressure: the system opposes the crowding by favouring the side with fewer gas moles — 2 moles of NH₃ against 4 moles of reactants — so the forward reaction is favoured and yield increases; hence high pressure is used industrially. (b) Increasing temperature: heat is effectively a product of the exothermic forward reaction, so the system opposes added heat by favouring the endothermic reverse reaction; ammonia decomposes and yield falls (and Kc itself decreases). (c) Removing ammonia: the system opposes the removal by producing more ammonia — the forward reaction is favoured continuously, which is why product is drawn off industrially. (d) Catalyst: speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position and yield are unchanged; equilibrium is merely reached sooner. Industry uses a moderate temperature (around 450 °C) as a compromise: low temperature gives the best equilibrium yield but an uneconomically slow rate, while high temperature gives speed but poor yield; with the catalyst providing an acceptable rate, a moderate temperature captures workable amounts of both.

questions.question: 1,0 mol of H₂ and 1,0 mol of I₂ are sealed in a 2 dm³ vessel at a fixed temperature. At equilibrium the vessel contains 1,6 mol of HI. Write the Kc expression for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, calculate Kc, interpret its value, and state what would and would not change Kc.
questions.expected_answer: Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]); no solids or pure liquids are involved, so all three gases appear. Moles table: forming 1,6 mol HI consumes 0,8 mol H₂ and 0,8 mol I₂ (ratio 2:1:1 from the equation), leaving 0,2 mol of each reactant at equilibrium. Concentrations (divide by the 2 dm³ volume): [H₂] = 0,1 mol·dm⁻³; [I₂] = 0,1 mol·dm⁻³; [HI] = 0,8 mol·dm⁻³. Kc = 0,8² ÷ (0,1 × 0,1) = 0,64 ÷ 0,01 = 64. Interpretation: Kc is much greater than 1, so the equilibrium lies well toward the products — the mixture is dominated by HI. Kc is constant at a given temperature: adding reactants or products, changing the pressure or volume, or adding a catalyst will shift concentrations but the ratio returns to the same Kc. Only a change in temperature changes Kc — for an exothermic forward reaction heating lowers Kc, for an endothermic one heating raises it.
